title: Sobolo
author: Afia Amoako
desc: The Ghanaian version of bissap, and traditionally on the spicy side — grains of selim, African nutmeg, cloves, peppercorn and grains of paradise.
longDesc: Sobolo is hibiscus steeped with a serious load of spice, and its author puts the difference plainly: this is the Ghanaian version of bissap, and in Ghana we pack in the spices. Fifteen grains of selim, seven African nutmegs, two tablespoons of cloves, two dried chillies, a tablespoon of black peppercorn and a teaspoon of grains of paradise are blended with a whole pineapple, a third of a cup of ginger and a cup of pitted dates. The pineapple skin and leaves go into the pot too. It steeps at a rolling boil for at least thirty minutes, uncovered so it does not splash, and makes fifteen cups.
ingredients: 1 pineapple, with its skin and leaves reserved
2 large thumbs, about 1/3 cup, ginger, peeled
16 cups water — see the note on this quantity
Sugar to taste, about 3/4 cup brown sugar
// The spices are all optional. See the author's substitution note.
equipment: Fine mesh strainer or nut-milk bag
steps: Soak the pineapple in water and vinegar 2 to 3 minutes, then cut it, reserving the skin and leaves.
Blend the pineapple flesh, ginger, spices and dates until smooth.
Put the pineapple leaves, the skin, the blended mixture and the spices into a pot with 10 cups of water and bring to the boil. Do not cover the pot, otherwise it will splash.
Add the sorrel and bring the heat down to allow the mixture to steep at a rolling boil.
Let it steep for at least 30 minutes, then turn off the stove.
Add the sugar a quarter cup at a time, to taste — about 3/4 cup of brown sugar in all.
Let it cool completely, to room temperature.
Strain through a fine mesh strainer or a nut-milk bag.
chefTips: Do not cover the pot. Her instruction and her reason — it will splash, and hibiscus stains everything it touches.
The pineapple SKIN and LEAVES go in the pot, not in the bin. That is where a lot of the flavour is and it is the detail most recipes omit.
Steep at a rolling boil for at least thirty minutes, not a simmer. Thirty is a floor, not a target.
Sugar a quarter cup at a time after the heat is off. Three quarters of a cup is where she landed, but hibiscus sourness varies with the batch.
Cool completely before straining. Hot hibiscus through a nut-milk bag is a burn waiting to happen and it strains cloudier.
All the spices are optional, by her own note: you can remove them entirely and replace them with an extra half tablespoon of cloves and two cinnamon sticks, or not replace them at all.
Be aware of a gap in the printed recipe — sixteen cups of water is listed but only ten go into the pot. The other six are never placed.
commonMistakes: Discarding the pineapple skin and leaves.
Simmering rather than holding a rolling boil.
All the sugar at once, while it is still hot.
sources: Adapted from 'Sobolo (Spiced Hibiscus Drink)', eatwithafia.com. Published 6 July 2020; modified 19 January 2026. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'support' — a generic account name, not a person. Yield as printed: '15 cups'. Total time as printed: '45 minutes'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

AN ATTRIBUTION INFERENCE, recorded as an inference and not as fact: bestofvegan.com captions a sobolo photo 'by Afia Amoako/The Canadian African', and thecanadianafrican.com bylines its recipes 'By Afia'. That points to one author, and Afia Amoako is credited in the display author field on that basis. THE NAME DOES NOT APPEAR ON THE SOURCE PAGE ITSELF, whose byline is the account name 'support'.

Ingredients exactly as printed, TWO-PASS: '1 pineapple'; '2 large thumbs ~1/3 cup of ginger peeled'; '15 grains of selim*'; '7 african nutmeg*'; '2 tbsp cloves'; '2 dried chillies*'; '1 tbsp black peppercorn'; '1 tsp grains of paradise*'; '1 cup dates pitted'; '2 cups hibiscus'; '16 cups water'; 'Sugar to taste'. The asterisks are the page's own, marking the West African spices.

THE GHANAIAN FRAMING, quoted verbatim and TWO-PASS, because it is the clearest statement of the sobolo-versus-bissap distinction in the record: 'Sobolo is the Ghanian version of Bissap, and is traditionally on the spicy side.' — spelling 'Ghanian' as printed. And: 'In Ghana, we pack in the spices ( I mean this is nothing new because we Ghanaians love heat).'

Method as printed: soak the pineapple in water and vinegar '2-3 minutes'; 'In a pot, add the pineapple leaves, skin, blended mixture, and spices with 10 cups of water and bring to a boil. Do not cover the pot otherwise it will splash'; 'add the sorrel and bring the heat down to allow the mixture to steep at a rolling boil'; 'Let it steep for at least 30 minutes, then turn off the stove'; cool 'completely cool (room temperature)' then strain.

SUGAR, two readings recorded: pass one gives 'approximately 3/4 cup of brown sugar, adding 1/4 at a time'; pass two gives it in the first person, 'I added ~ 3/4 cup'. The figure agrees; only the framing differs.
A GAP IN THE SOURCE, flagged and not corrected: '16 cups water' is listed in the ingredients but only 10 cups are placed in the method. The remaining 6 cups appear nowhere. No correction is asserted.

THE AUTHOR'S SUBSTITUTION NOTE, verbatim: 'All these spices are optional. You can completely remove them and replace with an additional 1/2 tbsp of cloves and 2 cinnamon sticks or not replace them at all.'
NOT FERMENTED. Sobolo is a steeped and refrigerated infusion. Note that the Nigerian zobo documented separately in this collection is the same hibiscus drink under its Hausa-derived name.

OTHER SOBOLO SOURCES EXAMINED AND THEIR PROBLEMS, all recorded rather than quietly dropped: thefooddictator.com's version is bylined 'The Generalissimo', a pseudonym, and names prekese and hwentia but no cloves, boiling '10-15 mins (Until water changes color)'; yen.com.gh's list is near-identical to the Food Dictator's — same cups, same syrup, same sugar, same boil time — and looks derivative, while its 'Spicy Sobolo' variant matches this Eat with Afia recipe and appears copied from it; an AVRDC print page carries NO title, byline, date or country and steeps 400 ml of boiling water over the calyces for '45 minutes to overnight' with no boil at all, with '5 ghwentia' ambiguous between 5 g and 5 grains; a GNA feature by Caleb Kuleke, 22 March 2026, gives no quantities but records that 'recipes vary between households' and that it is 'a soft drink at naming ceremonies, weddings, and funerals'; and a YES Abroad account is by a non-Ghanaian exchange student reporting her host family's practice, with no quantities.

UNRECONCILED ACROSS THE FIELD: this recipe boils and then steeps at least 30 minutes; the Food Dictator and YEN boil 10-15 minutes; AVRDC steeps 45 minutes to overnight without boiling. Three incompatible methods, recorded as such.
storage: Up to a week refrigerated in sealed bottles.
healthBenefits: Hibiscus calyces are very high in anthocyanins and vitamin C, and trials associate them with modest blood-pressure reduction.
Ginger, cloves and grains of paradise all carry documented anti-inflammatory compounds.
Vegan, caffeine-free and far lower in sugar than a commercial soft drink.
Dates sweeten while adding potassium and fibre.
culturalNote: Sobolo is poured at naming ceremonies, weddings and funerals, and it is the drink a Ghanaian household makes in a stockpot rather than a jug. The spicing is the point — fifteen grains of selim and seven African nutmegs is not a cautious recipe, and the author says as much.
